meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are generally the better persuaded by the reasons we discover ourselves than by those given to us by others'?
meta.ogDescription: The thought is genuinely Pascal’s — Pensées fragment 10, confirmed in the French. The popular English wording, though, has no traceable translator.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1623–1662 · French mathematician, physicist and religious philosopher
answer.sourceLine: The thought is genuinely Pascal’s: the French sits in the Pensées as Section I, fragment 10, and is easy to confirm. But this particular English wording is not the standard translation and matches no published edition we could source — it is an uncredited rendering that circulates through quotation aggregators. W. F. Trotter’s public-domain English reads “People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others.”

source.heading: The source: Pensées, Section I, fragment 10

docMeta.dd: Section I, “Thoughts on Mind and on Style” — fragment 10 in the Brunschvicg numbering
1670, posthumously — Pascal died in 1662 leaving the work unfinished
Popular wording: no identifiable translator or edition. Standard public-domain English: W. F. Trotter, in print by 1910.

source.excerpt:
On se persuade mieux, pour l’ordinaire, par les raisons qu’on a soi-même trouvées, que par celles qui sont venues dans l’esprit des autres.

“People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others.” — trans. W. F. Trotter
trail: The French is real and easy to check. Section I of the Brunschvicg edition ↗ carries it as fragment 10: “On se persuade mieux, pour l’ordinaire, par les raisons qu’on a soi-même trouvées, que par celles qui sont venues dans l’esprit des autres.”

The standard English reads differently. Project Gutenberg’s Trotter text ↗ gives fragment 10 as “People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others” — the same wording Wikiquote lists in its sourced Section I ↗.
Trotter’s rendering was in print well before 1931: the Internet Archive’s scan of the Harvard Classics volume ↗ (P. F. Collier & Son, 1910) prints fragment 10 in exactly that form.

The popular wording, by contrast, arrives with no edition at all. The Quotations Page ↗ credits it to “Michael Moncur’s (Cynical) Quotations” — a hobbyist compilation, not a translation — and supplies no translator, year, or page. No edition search turned up a published translation matching it.
source.excerptNote: Fragment 10 is a single free-standing sentence; there is no surrounding paragraph to quote, so this is the whole of it. The English given here is Trotter’s, the standard public-domain translation — not the smoother wording this page asks about, which matches no edition we could locate.

sourceLink.text: Pensées, éd. Brunschvicg, Section I, fragment 10 (French Wikisource)

source.rightsNote: Two things here have clear status and one does not. Pascal’s French (Pensées, 1670) is long out of copyright, and W. F. Trotter’s English translation was in print by 1910 ↗, comfortably before the 1931 US threshold, so it too is public domain — which is why Project Gutenberg hosts it ↗. The wording on this page, however, is neither of those: it is an English rendering with no traceable translator or edition, so we make no claim about its status. If you need Pascal’s thought in English you can reproduce freely, quote Trotter’s.

author.name: Blaise Pascal
author.heading: Who was Blaise Pascal?
author.metaLine: 1623–1662 · French mathematician, physicist and religious philosopher
author.bio: Blaise Pascal was a child prodigy who built a mechanical calculator at nineteen, proved that vacuums exist before he was twenty-five, and co-founded probability theory with Fermat at thirty-one. After a religious experience later that same year, 1654, he devoted himself to the Jansenist community at Port-Royal and began drafting a defence of Christian faith. He died at thirty-nine with that defence unfinished, leaving thousands of paper scraps that his family assembled and published in 1670 as the Pensées. Because the book is a pile of fragments rather than a finished argument, it has been renumbered by every major editor since — which is precisely why Pascal quotes drift so easily in English.

misattribution.heading: Right author, unsigned translation
misattribution.intro: This is not a case of a quote being stolen from someone else — Pascal really did write the sentence, in French, and it is easy to find. The problem is narrower and more common than outright fabrication: the English everyone shares is nobody’s in particular.

items.why: “We are generally the better persuaded by the reasons we discover ourselves than by those given to us by others” appears across quotation sites with no edition attached. The Quotations Page ↗ prints it crediting only “Michael Moncur’s (Cynical) Quotations” — no translator, no year, no page.

Trotter’s fragment 10 reads “People are generally better persuaded by the reasons which they have themselves discovered than by those which have come into the mind of others” — recognisably the same thought, audibly not the same sentence. Confirmed in Project Gutenberg’s text ↗.

items.who: Attributed by Today in Science to the H. F. Stewart edition
items.why: “We are generally more effectually persuaded by reasons we have ourselves discovered than by those which have occurred to others” is cited by Today in Science ↗ to H. F. Stewart (ed.), Pascal’s Pensées (1950), p. 11 — a mid-century edition, and a reminder that not every English Pascal is out of copyright.

misattribution.truthLine: Pascal wrote it, and you can read it in his own words: “On se persuade mieux, pour l’ordinaire, par les raisons qu’on a soi-même trouvées, que par celles qui sont venues dans l’esprit des autres” ↗. Credit the man — but if you need a citable English, use Trotter’s.

context.heading: Why the English keeps sliding around
lead: Pascal never published the Pensées. He died in 1662 leaving a mass of notes — some on scraps pinned together with thread — toward a book he never wrote. His family printed a tidied selection in 1670, and every editor since has re-sorted and re-numbered the fragments: Brunschvicg, Lafuma, Sellier, Le Guern each produce a different ordering of the same material. A Pascal citation that says only “Pensées” is therefore nearly uncheckable, which is exactly the gap quotation sites fall into.

The wording problem is separate and simpler. Fragment 10 is one plain French sentence, and plain French sentences invite loose Englishing. Trotter’s 1910 version is faithful but clunky; the version that went viral is smoother, shorter, and better balanced — and nobody signed it. Somewhere between an anthology and a website, someone improved the prose and the improvement stuck.
detailsBody: French Wikisource’s Brunschvicg text lists fragment 10 with a string of cross-references to earlier editors — B., 390; C., 357; P. R., XXIX, 26; Bos., I, x, 10; Faug., I, 173; Hav., VII, 10; Mol., II, 143; Mich., 435 — which is a compact illustration of how many times this one sentence has been renumbered.

Trotter translated from Brunschvicg’s arrangement, which is why his fragment 10 and Brunschvicg’s fragment 10 are the same sentence. Editions built on Lafuma or Sellier will number it differently, so “fragment 10” is only meaningful with the editor named alongside it.
context.pull: Pascal wrote the thought. He just never wrote it in these words.
